A research report · Rwanda and Uganda, 1957–2003

Paul Kagame’s Rise from Exile

A Tutsi refugee in Uganda, an officer in Museveni’s army, commander of the Rwandese Patriotic Front, and president of Rwanda

Prepared by Scholar · October 2026

This report follows Paul Kagame from a Rwandan refugee camp in Uganda to the presidency of Rwanda. It covers his childhood in exile, his years as an intelligence officer in Yoweri Museveni’s army, the founding of the Rwandese Patriotic Front (RPF), the war of 1990 to 1994, and the years from 1994 to 2003 in which he took full power.

The report gives the RPF’s own account and the account of its critics. Where they disagree, it names who says what. Dates and figures were checked against at least one source other than Wikipedia. Where that was not possible, the text says [unconfirmed]. Maps are schematic where marked. Photographs are free files from Wikimedia Commons; the photographs you asked for that are not free are linked in section 9.

1The report

From Nshungerezi to Kigali

Nine sections · about 60–80 minutes · 2 maps, 12 images, 9 archive links

1. A refugee childhood, 1957–1976

Key dates
  1. 23 Oct 1957Born at Tambwe, southern Rwanda
  2. Nov 1959Violence against Tutsi begins
  3. 1961–62Family crosses into Uganda
  4. 1 Jul 1962Rwanda independent
  5. 1972–76Ntare School, Mbarara

Paul Kagame was born on 23 October 1957 at Tambwe, a village in what is now the Southern Province of Rwanda. The date and place are given in Encyclopedia.com’s biography and in Kagame’s own interviews with François Soudan. Time also gives Tambwe and the year 1957. He was the youngest of six children. His father, Deogratias Rutagambwa, was a Tutsi businessman, and both parents were related to the Rwandan royal family.

Rwanda was then a United Nations trust territory under Belgian administration. In November 1959 a Hutu uprising, which the new Hutu leadership called the “social revolution,” began. Tutsi homes were burned and many Tutsi were killed. By the time Rwanda became independent on 1 July 1962, about 200,000 Tutsi had left the country, according to Katy Long’s study of British archives (Journal of Eastern African Studies, 2012). The Kagame family first moved north, to the Mutara area near the Ugandan border, and then crossed into Uganda. The sources give the crossing as 1960 or 1961.

The family settled in a refugee camp in 1962. Most accounts, including Encyclopedia.com and Wikipedia, name the camp as Nshungerezi. Time (2012) names it as Gahunge, “in southwest Uganda.” The district is also given in two ways: Encyclopedia.com and Wikipedia say Toro, while a memoir in Rwanda’s New Times places Nshungerezi in south-eastern Uganda. This report could not find a published coordinate for Nshungerezi, so the map marks only the general area, in Isingiro, near the Nakivale and Oruchinga settlements. The exact location is [unconfirmed].

The wider picture is clearer. The Berghahn study of refugee rights by Guglielmo Verdirame and Barbara Harrell-Bond says that between 1959 and 1967 about 78,000 Tutsi refugees came to south-western Uganda. They were settled in the Oruchinga valley in 1961 and at Nakivale in 1962, then at Kahunge, Kyaka, Ibuga and Rwamwanja in Toro, and from 1965 at Kyangwali and Kinyara in Bunyoro. UNHCR records that Oruchinga opened as a transit center in 1959. It was in this camp world that Kagame met Fred Rwigyema, who was a few years older. Rwigyema later led the RPF.

Kagame went to a camp school, then to Rwengoro Primary School, and then to Ntare School in Mbarara. Rwanda’s KT Press and Kagame’s own website give his years at Ntare as 1972 to 1976. In a 2015 speech Kagame said the school was “another home away from refugee camps.” He was later suspended from Ntare, by his own account after fights with students who insulted Rwandans, and he finished at Old Kampala Secondary School.

Why it matters

Kagame grew up stateless. Rwandan refugees in Uganda could not easily become citizens, and after 1962 Ugandan politicians often treated them as a threat. Many scholars, among them Mamdani and Otunnu, argue that this exclusion explains why so many young refugees joined Uganda’s armed movements, and later why they wanted to return to Rwanda by force.

2. Soldier in Uganda’s wars, 1979–1986

Key dates
  1. 1979Joins Museveni’s FRONASA
  2. Apr 1979Amin overthrown
  3. Dec 1980Disputed Ugandan election
  4. 6 Feb 1981Kabamba attack opens the Bush War
  5. 26 Jan 1986NRA takes Kampala

In 1979 Kagame and Rwigyema joined the Front for National Salvation (FRONASA), the armed group of Yoweri Museveni, which fought with Tanzanian forces to overthrow Idi Amin. The BBC and CBC profiles both give 1979 as the year Kagame joined. Amin fell in April 1979. After the disputed election of December 1980 returned Milton Obote to power, Museveni went to war against the government.

The war began on 6 February 1981 with an attack on the Kabamba military barracks. Uganda’s Daily Monitor, in its history of how the war was planned, reports that the group had about 41 men but only 27 guns, which is the origin of the phrase “the original 27.” The Independent (Uganda) and ChimpReports list Rwigyema among the original group, and the Monitor says Kagame led a small team armed with pistols. The exact membership of the “27” is still argued in Ugandan sources. The attack did not capture the armory, but the force withdrew with some weapons. It became the National Resistance Army (NRA), and it fought a guerrilla war, mainly in the Luweero area north of Kampala.

Kagame worked in intelligence in the NRA. When the NRA captured Kampala on 26 January 1986 and Museveni became president, Kagame became head of military intelligence; some accounts say acting head. The BBC’s 2003 profile gives the 1986 appointment. Rwigyema rose higher. He became a senior commander of the Ugandan army and a deputy minister of defense. Several thousand Rwandan refugees served in the NRA, but published figures differ, and this report does not give one.

Why it matters

The bush war gave the future RPF a trained officer corps, combat experience, and close contacts inside Uganda’s new government. It also made the Rwandan refugees visible in Ugandan politics. Their opponents in Uganda then used their role in the NRA against them.

3. From RANU to the RPF, and Fort Leavenworth, 1979–1990

Key dates
  1. 1979RANU founded in Nairobi
  2. Dec 1987RANU becomes the RPF in Kampala
  3. 1989–90Rwandan officers lose posts in Uganda
  4. 1990Kagame at Fort Leavenworth

The political organization came before the army. The Rwandese Alliance for National Unity (RANU) was founded in 1979 by Rwandan refugees, with its first headquarters in Nairobi. In December 1987, at its congress in Kampala, RANU renamed itself the Rwandese Patriotic Front (RPF). These dates are given by the Rwandan government’s official history and by the RPF’s anniversary material, and they agree with Wm. Cyrus Reed’s 1996 article in the Journal of Modern African Studies. Reed describes the RPF as a movement that tried to present itself as national rather than Tutsi, with a program against corruption and for the return of refugees.

By 1989 the position of Rwandan-born officers in Uganda had become weaker. Ugandan critics complained that “foreigners” held senior posts. Rwigyema was removed from his senior positions. Prunier and Otunnu both argue that this pressure, and the Habyarimana government’s refusal to accept a large return of refugees, pushed the RPF to plan an invasion. Otunnu’s chapter in The Path of a Genocide (1999) is the most detailed study of how the invasion was prepared inside the Ugandan army.

In 1990 Kagame went to the United States Army Command and General Staff College at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. CNN (2008) and other accounts agree that he was there when the RPF invaded Rwanda on 1 October. He left the course in mid-October 1990 and returned to East Africa. The exact day he left is given differently in different accounts and is [unconfirmed]. No free photograph of Kagame at Fort Leavenworth was found. See the archive links in section 9.

Why it matters

The RPF was a political movement before it was an army, and it had many members abroad. Its leaders had also learned a model in Uganda: a disciplined rebel army with a political program could take a state. Kagame’s training in the United States in 1990 later gave rise to many claims about American support for the RPF. The sources used here show only that he attended the course.

4. The invasion and the retreat to the Virunga, October 1990–1992

Key dates
  1. 1 Oct 1990RPF crosses at Kagitumba
  2. 2 Oct 1990Rwigyema killed
  3. Oct 1990French and Zairean troops arrive
  4. Oct–Nov 1990Kagame takes command
  5. 23 Jan 1991Raid on Ruhengeri

On 1 October 1990 RPF fighters, most of them soldiers who had left the Ugandan army with their weapons, crossed the border at Kagitumba, in the far north-east of Rwanda. The staging area was on the Ugandan side, near Mirama Hills. Rwigyema was killed on 2 October, the second day. How he died is disputed; see section 8. Two other senior commanders, Peter Bayingana and Chris Bunyenyezi, were killed later that month. Accounts of their deaths also differ.

The Rwandan government asked for help. France sent troops to Kigali in early October 1990 to protect French citizens and the airport. Zaire sent troops who fought in the north-east. The RPF advanced south as far as the Gabiro area and then was driven back. By the end of October the invasion had failed as a conventional attack.

Kagame returned and took command. He moved the surviving force west into the Virunga volcanoes on the border with Uganda and Zaire, where the forests and high, cold ground gave cover. He rebuilt it as a guerrilla army. Kinzer and Waugh describe this period, from the RPF side, as the time when Kagame imposed strict discipline and reorganized the army. On 23 January 1991 the RPF raided Ruhengeri, the main town of the north-west. It held the town for a day, freed prisoners from the prison, including the jailed former intelligence chief Théoneste Lizinde, and then withdrew.

In 1991 and 1992 the RPF fought a war of raids along the northern border and slowly gained a strip of territory. Its headquarters moved to Mulindi, near the Ugandan border north of Byumba. Inside Rwanda, Tutsi civilians were arrested and killed in several local massacres between 1990 and 1993. Human Rights Watch and Des Forges document these massacres. Negotiations between the government and the RPF began in 1992.

Why it matters

The first defeat made Kagame the leader of the RPF. The army he rebuilt in the Virunga was smaller, more disciplined and more centralized, and it was loyal to him. The war also changed Rwanda. The government used the invasion to accuse all Tutsi inside the country of supporting the enemy, and that language later became part of the propaganda of the genocide.

5. The 1993 offensive and the Arusha Accords

Key dates
  1. 8 Feb 1993RPF offensive in the north
  2. Feb 1993Halt about 30 km from Kigali
  3. 4 Aug 1993Arusha Accords signed
  4. 5 Oct 1993UNAMIR created
  5. 28 Dec 1993600 RPF troops enter the CND building

On 8 February 1993 the RPF broke a ceasefire and attacked in the north, around Byumba and Ruhengeri. The RPF said the attack was a response to killings of Tutsi in the north-west in January 1993. The offensive came within about 30 kilometers of Kigali before it stopped. The National Security Archive’s collection on the Arusha Accords documents the attack and the diplomatic pressure that followed. France sent more troops. The offensive drove a very large number of Hutu civilians from the north; Des Forges and other sources give figures for the displaced, which differ.

The Arusha Accords were signed on 4 August 1993. They provided for a broad transitional government, the return of refugees, and a single army, in which the RPF would have a large share of the officers. The United Nations Security Council created the UN Assistance Mission for Rwanda (UNAMIR), under the Canadian general Roméo Dallaire, on 5 October 1993. On 28 December 1993 UNAMIR escorted a battalion of about 600 RPF soldiers into Kigali. They were placed in the parliament building, the Conseil National de Développement (CND), to protect RPF politicians who were to join the transitional government. That government was never installed.

Why it matters

The 1993 offensive showed that the RPF could probably defeat the Rwandan army. Supporters of the RPF describe Arusha as a fair settlement that Hutu extremists sabotaged. Critics such as Kuperman argue that the RPF’s military pressure and its large gains at Arusha frightened the regime and its extremists. Both views appear in the scholarship, and the report does not choose between them.

6. April to July 1994

Key dates
  1. 6 Apr 1994Habyarimana’s plane shot down
  2. 7 Apr 1994Killings begin; RPF in the CND fights out
  3. 22 Jun 1994French Operation Turquoise
  4. 4 Jul 1994RPF takes Kigali
  5. 17–18 JulGisenyi falls
  6. 19 Jul 1994New government sworn in

On the evening of 6 April 1994 a Falcon 50 jet carrying President Habyarimana and President Cyprien Ntaryamira of Burundi was shot down by missiles as it approached Kigali airport. Everyone on board died. Who fired the missiles is disputed; see section 8. Within hours, members of the Presidential Guard, soldiers and Interahamwe militia began killing Tutsi and Hutu opponents of the regime. The prime minister, Agathe Uwilingiyimana, was killed on 7 April. Over about one hundred days, about 800,000 people were killed, according to the United Nations figure. Human Rights Watch (Des Forges, 1999) estimated at least 500,000 Tutsi.

The RPF battalion in the CND building fought its way out on 7 April, and the main RPF army attacked from the north. Kagame refused UN and other proposals for a ceasefire that would leave the government forces in place. Supporters of the RPF say that only an RPF victory could stop the genocide. Critics say the RPF put winning the war ahead of rescuing civilians. One RPF column moved south down the eastern side of the country, through Rwamagana and Kibungo, and then turned west toward Butare. Other units encircled Kigali. Gitarama, where the interim government had moved, fell in June. Butare was taken in early July; the exact date is [unconfirmed].

The RPF took Kigali on 4 July 1994. Rwanda now marks 4 July as Liberation Day. On 22 June, France had begun Operation Turquoise, under a UN mandate, and set up a protected zone in the south-west. The government army and very large numbers of civilians fled west into Zaire. Gisenyi, on the border with Goma, fell on 17 or 18 July. Sources give both dates: a French military intelligence note dated 18 July says the RPF had entered the town. The RPF declared a ceasefire on 18 July.

On 19 July 1994 a Government of National Unity was sworn in. Pasteur Bizimungu, a Hutu member of the RPF, became president. Faustin Twagiramungu, a Hutu politician from the opposition, became prime minister. Kagame became vice president and minister of defense, a post that had not existed under the Arusha Accords.

Why it matters

The RPF’s victory ended the genocide in the territory it controlled. The same months also produced the mass flight into Zaire, and the armed camps on the border led to the wars in Congo from 1996. Questions about RPF conduct in 1994, and about the plane, are still part of Rwandan and international politics.

7. Consolidation of power, 1994–2003

Key dates
  1. 19 Jul 1994Kagame vice president and defense minister
  2. 23 Mar 2000Bizimungu resigns
  3. 17 Apr 2000Elected president, 81 votes to 5
  4. 22 Apr 2000Sworn in
  5. 25 Aug 2003Wins first direct election, 95.05%

From 1994 to 2000 Bizimungu was president, but the BBC wrote in April 2000 that Kagame “has effectively ruled the country for six years.” Several leading Hutu members of the government left office and some went into exile, among them Twagiramungu and the interior minister Seth Sendashonga in 1995. Sendashonga was killed in Nairobi in 1998.

Bizimungu resigned on 23 March 2000. The US State Department’s human rights report for 2000 gives that date. IRIN reported on 30 March that the Supreme Court had ruled that Vice President Kagame should act as president. On 17 April 2000 a joint session of the Transitional National Assembly and the cabinet elected Kagame president. IRIN reported the vote as 81 of 86, with five votes for the other RPF nominee. The BBC reported that Kagame was sworn in on 22 April 2000 at Amahoro Stadium.

A new constitution was approved in 2003. In the presidential election of 25 August 2003 Kagame received 95.05 percent of the vote and Twagiramungu 3.62 percent, according to the European Union observer mission’s report and IFES. The EU mission reported irregularities, and the BBC reported its view that the election was not entirely fair.

Why it matters

The years from 1994 to 2003 turned a rebel commander into an elected head of state. Supporters point to order, reconstruction and economic growth. Critics such as Reyntjens and Wrong describe the same years as the creation of a one-party state in which rivals were removed, some by exile and some by killing.

8. Contested questions

The scholarship on Kagame and the RPF is divided. The list below states each claim and who makes it. The report does not decide between them.

How Rwigyema died

The RPF’s account is that Rwigyema was killed by enemy fire on 2 October 1990. Gérard Prunier, in The Rwanda Crisis (1995), reported that he was shot by one of his own officers after a dispute about strategy. Michela Wrong (2021) discusses the accounts again. No official inquiry has been published.

Killings by the RPF, 1990–1994

In 1994 a UNHCR team led by Robert Gersony visited 91 sites in Rwanda and refugee camps in neighboring countries. According to Human Rights Watch (Des Forges, 1999), Gersony estimated that the RPF killed between 25,000 and 45,000 people from April to August 1994. No full written report was released; a UNHCR summary of his presentation to the UN Commission of Experts, dated 10–11 October 1994, has since been published. The Rwandan government in 1994 accepted that some soldiers had carried out reprisal killings, but it rejected the scale and the claim that the killings were systematic. Des Forges wrote that HRW had too little data to confirm or revise the estimate, but that it was more likely accurate than claims of hundreds of thousands. Judi Rever (2018) argues that RPF killings were far larger and organized from the top. Supporters of the RPF and several reviewers reject Rever’s conclusions and warn that such claims are used by those who deny the genocide.

Who shot down the plane

In 2006 the French judge Jean-Louis Bruguière concluded that the RPF had shot down the plane on Kagame’s order, and he issued arrest warrants for nine of Kagame’s associates. Rwanda broke relations with France. A Rwandan government inquiry, the Mutsinzi report (published January 2010), concluded that the missiles were fired from the area of the Kanombe military camp, held by the Rwandan army. In January 2012 the French judges Marc Trévidic and Nathalie Poux presented an expert report, based on a visit to Kigali in 2010, which found that the missiles were most likely fired from the Kanombe camp or near it. Reuters and franceinfo reported that this report did not name the people who fired. Prosecutors asked for the case to be closed for lack of evidence in October 2018, and the judges dismissed it on 21 December 2018, according to the BBC. Filip Reyntjens and some other scholars continue to consider the RPF the more likely author. Others, including Linda Melvern, attribute the attack to Hutu extremists.

Did the RPF invasion provoke the genocide?

Alan Kuperman (2004) argues that the RPF’s attacks made extremist violence more likely and that its leaders accepted this risk. Mamdani (2001) also treats the 1990 invasion as a turning point. Kinzer (2008) and the RPF reply that the genocide was planned by the regime, and that the RPF was the only force that stopped it.

9. Photographs that could not be embedded

You asked for photographs of Kagame in the Ugandan army, at Fort Leavenworth, of RPF forces during the war, and of the entry into Kigali in 1994. This report looked for free files on Wikimedia Commons. It found:

  • Kagame in the Ugandan army (1979–1990): no free photograph found.
  • Kagame at Fort Leavenworth (1990): no free photograph found.
  • RPF forces in the field, 1990–1994: no free photograph found. The report uses two 2024 photographs of official markers at Kagitumba and Gikoba and a 2022 photograph of a monument instead, and says so in each caption.
  • The RPF entry into Kigali, July 1994: no free photograph found. The nearest free photograph is Kagame with William Perry on 31 July 1994.

Photographs of these subjects exist in press agencies and archives. They are under copyright, so they are linked, not copied. The links open search pages or the archive’s home page. Some sites require an account to see full images.

  1. Getty Images: “paul kagame 1994” — editorial agency photographs, including AFP pictures of RPF soldiers and of Kagame in 1994. Try also “Rwandan Patriotic Front 1994” and “Kigali July 1994.”
  2. AP Newsroom (Associated Press) — AP photographs from Rwanda, 1990–1994. Search “Kagame 1994” or “Rwandan Patriotic Front.” Requires an account.
  3. Reuters Connect — the Reuters picture archive, with photographs of the RPF advance and of Kigali in July 1994. Requires an account.
  4. US Army Command and General Staff College, digital library — the CGSC’s Combined Arms Research Library; the place to ask about class records and photographs from 1990.
  5. Genocide Archive of Rwanda — the Aegis Trust and Kigali Genocide Memorial archive of photographs, video testimony and documents.
  6. Kigali Genocide Memorial — the memorial’s site, with its exhibitions and contact for the archive.
  7. UN Photo — United Nations photographs, including UNAMIR in Kigali, 1993–1994.
  8. ICRC audiovisual archives — Red Cross photographs from Rwanda and the refugee camps in 1994.
  9. Paul Kagame’s official Flickr account — the Rwandan presidency’s photographs. Mostly after 2000. Check the license on each photograph before reuse.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1Where and when was Kagame born, and how did his family come to live in Uganda?
Answer. He was born on 23 October 1957 at Tambwe in southern Rwanda. After the violence against Tutsi that began in November 1959, the family moved north and crossed into Uganda in 1960 or 1961 (sources differ). They settled in a refugee camp in 1962. Most sources name it Nshungerezi; Time names it Gahunge.
2What was “the original 27,” and what does the Daily Monitor say about the number?
Answer. It is the name for the group that attacked Kabamba barracks on 6 February 1981 and began Museveni’s Bush War. The Monitor says there were about 41 men but only 27 guns. Rwigyema and Kagame are listed among them, but the membership is still argued in Ugandan sources.
3What was RANU, and when did it become the RPF?
Answer. The Rwandese Alliance for National Unity, founded by refugees in 1979 with its headquarters in Nairobi. At its congress in Kampala in December 1987 it renamed itself the Rwandese Patriotic Front.
4Why was Kagame not with the RPF when it invaded on 1 October 1990, and what happened next?
Answer. He was at the US Army Command and General Staff College at Fort Leavenworth. Rwigyema was killed on 2 October. Kagame left the course in mid-October, returned, took command, and moved the defeated army into the Virunga volcanoes to rebuild it as a guerrilla force.
5What did the RPF do at Ruhengeri on 23 January 1991?
Answer. It raided the town, held it for a day, freed prisoners from the prison, including Théoneste Lizinde, and withdrew.
6What was the CND building, and why were RPF soldiers there in April 1994?
Answer. The parliament building in Kigali. Under the Arusha Accords, UNAMIR escorted a battalion of about 600 RPF soldiers there on 28 December 1993 to protect RPF politicians who were to join the transitional government. The battalion fought its way out on 7 April 1994.
7What did Gersony estimate, and how did the Rwandan government respond?
Answer. According to Human Rights Watch, he estimated that the RPF killed 25,000 to 45,000 people from April to August 1994. The government accepted that some soldiers had carried out reprisal killings but rejected the scale and the claim that the killings were systematic. No full written report was released.
8How did the French investigation into the plane change between 2006 and 2018?
Answer. In 2006 Judge Bruguière blamed the RPF and issued warrants against nine Kagame associates. In January 2012 the expert report for Judges Trévidic and Poux found that the missiles were most likely fired from or near the Kanombe army camp. The case was dismissed on 21 December 2018 for lack of evidence. Scholars still disagree about who fired.

Bibliography

All entries were checked against a publisher, library or journal record in October 2026. They are grouped by type. Read at least one book from the RPF side and one critical book.

Biographies and accounts close to Kagame

  • Colin M. Waugh, Paul Kagame and Rwanda: Power, Genocide and the Rwandan Patriotic Front (Jefferson, NC: McFarland, 2004). A detailed, sympathetic biography; good on the Uganda years.
  • Stephen Kinzer, A Thousand Hills: Rwanda’s Rebirth and the Man Who Dreamed It (Hoboken, NJ: Wiley, 2008). A journalist’s biography based on long interviews with Kagame; the most readable RPF-side account.
  • François Soudan, Kagame: The President of Rwanda Speaks (New York: Enigma Books, 2015). Interviews recorded in Kigali in 2013–2014; Kagame’s own account of his childhood and the war.
  • Yoweri Museveni, Sowing the Mustard Seed (London: Macmillan, 1997). Museveni’s memoir of FRONASA and the Bush War.

The war and the genocide

  • Gérard Prunier, The Rwanda Crisis: History of a Genocide (New York: Columbia University Press, 1995; 2nd ed. 1997). The standard early history; detailed on the RPF in Uganda and the 1990 invasion.
  • Alison Des Forges, Leave None to Tell the Story: Genocide in Rwanda (New York: Human Rights Watch, 1999). The fullest documentary study; also covers RPF killings and the Gersony findings. Online at HRW.
  • Roméo Dallaire, Shake Hands with the Devil: The Failure of Humanity in Rwanda (Toronto: Random House Canada, 2003). The UNAMIR commander’s memoir, including his meetings with Kagame.
  • Linda Melvern, A People Betrayed: The Role of the West in Rwanda’s Genocide (London: Zed Books, 2000). On the failure of the UN and Western governments.
  • Philip Gourevitch, We Wish to Inform You That Tomorrow We Will Be Killed with Our Families (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1998). Reporting from Rwanda after 1994, with interviews with Kagame.
  • Bruce D. Jones, Peacemaking in Rwanda: The Dynamics of Failure (Boulder: Lynne Rienner, 2001). The Arusha negotiations.

Refugees, origins of the RPF, and regional politics

  • Ogenga Otunnu, “An Historical Analysis of the Invasion by the Rwanda Patriotic Army (RPA),” in Howard Adelman and Astri Suhrke (eds.), The Path of a Genocide: The Rwanda Crisis from Uganda to Zaire (New Brunswick: Transaction, 1999), pp. 31–50. The refugees in Uganda and the preparation of the invasion.
  • Wm. Cyrus Reed, “Exile, Reform, and the Rise of the Rwandan Patriotic Front,” Journal of Modern African Studies 34, no. 3 (1996): 479–501. How RANU became the RPF and how it presented itself.
  • Katy Long, “Rwanda’s first refugees: Tutsi exile and international response 1959–64,” Journal of Eastern African Studies 6, no. 2 (2012): 211–229. British archives on the first refugees in Uganda.
  • Mahmood Mamdani, When Victims Become Killers: Colonialism, Nativism, and the Genocide in Rwanda (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2001). Argues that the citizenship crisis of Banyarwanda in Uganda shaped the RPF.
  • Gérard Prunier, Africa’s World War: Congo, the Rwandan Genocide, and the Making of a Continental Catastrophe (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009). The wars after 1994.

Critical studies

  • Alan J. Kuperman, “Provoking genocide: a revised history of the Rwandan Patriotic Front,” Journal of Genocide Research 6, no. 1 (2004): 61–84. Argues that RPF strategy made the genocide more likely.
  • Filip Reyntjens, Political Governance in Post-Genocide Rwanda (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2013). A critical study of RPF rule after 1994.
  • Michela Wrong, Do Not Disturb: The Story of a Political Murder and an African Regime Gone Bad (London: Fourth Estate, 2021). Through the 2013 murder of the former intelligence chief Patrick Karegeya; critical of Kagame, with much on the RPF’s years in Uganda.
  • Judi Rever, In Praise of Blood: The Crimes of the Rwandan Patriotic Front (Toronto: Random House Canada, 2018). Alleges large, organized RPF killings; strongly disputed.

Documents on the contested questions

  • Human Rights Watch, “The Rwandan Patriotic Front”, chapter of Leave None to Tell the Story. The source used here for the Gersony estimate.
  • UNHCR, summary of Gersony’s presentation to the UN Commission of Experts, 10–11 October 1994, as published in 2010.
  • Expert report for Judges Trévidic and Poux, “Rapport d’expertise,” 5 January 2012 (French).
  • National Security Archive, “Rwanda: The Failure of the Arusha Peace Accords”. Declassified documents on 1993–1994.

Data and map sources

  • Basemap: Natural Earth (public domain), 1:50m land and countries, 1:10m lakes and rivers, drawn with the Albers map engine built for The House of Timur. Borders are today’s borders.
  • Places: English Wikipedia coordinates, retrieved 21 October 2026. Gabiro and Mulindi were placed by hand and are labeled approximate. Nshungerezi is labeled by district only.
  • Routes: schematic lines through named places. They are not routes recorded on the ground.
  • Checking: each date and figure in the text was compared with at least one source other than Wikipedia (for example IRIN, the BBC, the US State Department, Human Rights Watch, the National Security Archive, Reuters, franceinfo, the EU observer report, the Daily Monitor, Encyclopedia.com and Time). Items that could not be checked are marked [unconfirmed].
